# Cracktro slide list

The single ordered list of slides, in reading order. Slides are linked by their stable Id (`#<id>`), never by position: the deck is a grid of bands and columns, so numbers shift whenever a slide is added or moved. Never write slide numbers anywhere; refer to a slide by its Id or heading (and CSS prefix). Legacy `#N` links still open the Nth slide and are rewritten to its `#<id>`.

Columns (one table, one row per line; `|` is not allowed inside a cell):

- **Id**: the slide's permanent link anchor (`#<id>`), lowercase kebab-case. The runtime slugs the heading (lines joined by spaces) unless the slide object sets `id`. Never change a published Id: when you reword a heading, set `id` on the slide object in `deck.js` to keep the old one. Pick the Id when adding a slide.
- **Heading**: the slide's first heading text, exactly as rendered.
- **Notes**: empty, or `illustrative` when the speaker notes must match `/illustrative|synthetic|simulated/i`.
- **Summary**: one public sentence with the slide's executive takeaway. Start band headers with `Band header (<band>):`. Describe the durable point, not measured counts or dates that age. No URLs, handles or slide numbers.

`docs/src/lib/cracktro/slides.js` parses this file and fails on a malformed row, an invalid Id, an empty Heading or Summary, an unknown Notes value or a duplicate. The docs build injects every row into the talk page's JSON-LD (`hasPart`: position, name, description, `#<id>` URL); `docs/tests/talk.spec.ts` checks the deck's ids, headings and that metadata against this list.

Editing: add, remove or move one row per slide in the same change as `deck.js`, and rewrite the Summary whenever the slide's message changes.

| security | Security |  | Band header (Security): design every workflow as if the agent is already compromised. |
| agentic-attacks | Agentic attacks | illustrative | Common agent attacks, from prompt injection to secret exfiltration and destructive commands, are each stopped by one or more layered defenses. |
| safety-and-control | Safety and control |  | Inputs are filtered, the agent runs sandboxed with a read-only token behind a firewall and gateway, and writes happen only through scanned safe outputs. |
| integrity-filtering | Integrity filtering | illustrative | Malicious comments on a public pull request never reach the agent: the MCP gateway rates each item by its author's trust and drops everything below the configured minimum integrity before the model sees it. |
| zero-secret-agents | Zero-secret agents | illustrative | The agent runs in an isolated sandbox, here the experimental micro-VM runtime, holding no credentials; every key stays on the host behind the MCP gateway, API proxy and egress firewall. |
| supply-chain-hardening | Supply chain hardening | illustrative | The compiler applies layered static checks, including trigger admission, expression safety, pinned actions, least privilege and secret scans, before any workflow runs. |
| safe-outputs | Safe outputs | illustrative | Agents only propose writes; threat detection reviews each proposal and a separate, scoped job applies only the declared outputs. |
| model-checked | Model-checked | illustrative | A bounded TLA+ model of the compiled workflow lets TLC check every job schedule against security invariants; seeded faults must break exactly one invariant, and witnesses prove validated writes still happen, shown as a replayed counterexample and witness trace across the job lanes. |
| need-to-know-enclaves | Need-to-know enclaves | illustrative | Experimental: single-use, isolated enclave agents read private repositories and return only schema-constrained values, so private data cannot leak into public replies. |
| continuous-red-teaming | Continuous Red Teaming | illustrative | A daily red-team agent keeps trying new ways to escape the agent firewall, and each escape it finds is turned into a firewall fix. |
| stop-manually-translating-intent-into-code | Stop manually translating intent into code. |  | The factory mindset: engineer processes that create trusted features instead of hand-translating intent into code. |
| human-agent-processes | Human agent processes |  | Band header (Human agent processes): engineer processes, not code, with patterns that pair people and agents, some with a column of worked examples below. |
| event-driven-hand-offs | Event-driven Hand-offs | illustrative | Event-driven hand-off patterns such as IssueOps, DailyOps, ReviewOps and LabelOps let agents do the work while people make the decisions. |
| repo-commands | Repo Commands | illustrative | Slash commands and label commands are synthetic triggers: one front matter line compiles into the real issue, comment, pull request and discussion events with a first-word guard, role check, reaction and status comment, so people call an agent exactly when they want it and can run it again. |
| labelops-state-machines | LabelOps state machines | illustrative | Labels become the states of a process: replace-label swaps one state for the next, allowed-transitions limits agents to declared edges, and label commands let people with the triage role drive the human steps without push or merge access. |

| ponytail-reviewer | Ponytail Reviewer | illustrative | A read-only agentic reviewer reads each ready pull request only for unnecessary complexity, posts one-line findings with the lines each saves, and says ship once nothing is left to cut; measured on gh-aw, most ready pull requests are already lean and most findings get acted on. |
| issue-monster | Issue Monster | illustrative | Issue Monster loves cookie issues: agents file their follow-ups into a cookie-labelled issue queue; a scheduler runs cheap deterministic gates and filters every few minutes and only wakes an agent to assign the best few issues to Copilot. |
| decide-draft-record | Decide · Draft · Record | illustrative | When a ready pull request carries an architecture decision with no record, an agent drafts an ADR that people finalize and merge with the code, and later agents read it to learn why the feature works that way. |
| pr-sous-chef | PR Sous Chef | illustrative | PR Sous Chef regularly finds pull requests that sit idle with work waiting, such as unresolved review comments or failing CI, and nudges Copilot to pick them back up, while humans still review and merge. |
| issues-as-intent | Issues as intent | illustrative | Contributors run a debug agent on their own failures and file anonymized issues that state intent, which maintainers plan and assign to Copilot. |
| daily-improvers | Daily Improvers | illustrative | Scheduled research agents find problems such as duplicated code, assign them to Copilot, and developers refine the resulting pull requests. |
| repo-assist | Repo Assist | illustrative | A scheduled assistant picks maintenance tasks such as triage and stale pull requests, a maintainer reviews every result, and backlogs shrink. |
| research-assign-observe | Research · Assign · Observe | illustrative | A daily benchmark agent files performance regressions, Copilot fixes them, and the next run observes the result to close the loop. |

| query-ask-grow | Query · Ask · Grow | illustrative | An expert DevOps agent read live telemetry through observability MCP servers and filed the most important instrumentation gap each day, growing OpenTelemetry support. |
| semantic-clustering | Semantic clustering | illustrative | Grouping functions by intent rather than by text exposes misplaced code that duplicate detection misses, and Copilot moves it. |

| mine-refine-apply | Mine · Refine · Apply | illustrative | Recurring review corrections are mined into Go linters, refined through review, and applied across the repository. |
| explore-reuse-lint | Explore · Reuse · Lint | illustrative | A daily code-analysis agent keeps a strategy cache to balance reusing proven strategies with exploring new ones, and every pattern it finds becomes a linter. |
| scan-fix-learn | Scan · Fix · Learn | illustrative | The .NET runtime team's CI health loop: a scanner files known build errors, a fixer attempts fixes, and a feedback agent tunes both. |

| speech-to-agent | Speech To Agent | illustrative | A dictation glossary maps misheard speech-to-text phrases to exact identifiers, so spoken prompts produce terms agents can grep. |
| for-pms | For PMs | illustrative | Agentic workflows also serve product managers: an existing team habit triggers an agent, which leaves an artifact for a human to decide on. |
| if-every-pr-needs-deep-human-review-you-dont-trust-your-process | If every PR needs deep human review, you don’t trust your process. | illustrative | Trust the process: if every pull request needs deep human review, improve checks, agent reviewers and tests until a skim is enough. |
| cost-optimization | Cost Optimization |  | Band header (Cost Optimization): debug, spend less and route smarter. |
| cost-management | Cost management | illustrative | Cut agent spend by scheduling less often, fetching data in deterministic steps, capping credits, using sub-agents and routing models with experimental model routing. |
| cost-guardrails | Cost guardrails | illustrative | Layered guardrails stop runaway agents: execution controls, including the experimental user rate limit, throttle events, the daily budget blocks runs before activation, per-run limits hard-stop a run, and optional central admission approves or denies each run before it starts. |
| budget-steering | Budget steering | illustrative | As a run nears its AI-credit or time budget, the firewall's API proxy appends a notice to the end of the agent's next model request saying what is left and what to do, once per conversation, so the agent submits what it has before the hard stop and audit records every delivery. |
| model-routing | Model routing | illustrative | Experimental: with model: router, each run gets the cheapest model and reasoning effort that is good enough for its task and stakes, and audit shows why. |
| deterministic-ops | DeterministicOps | illustrative | A dial runs from 100% agentic to fully deterministic: run history shows the same prompt lines becoming the same data-gathering calls every run, audit flags them, and translating them into steps: commands that write a file the agent reads turns the dial toward deterministic and cuts token use. |
| cli-vs-mcp | CLI vs MCP | illustrative | A fat MCP call such as listing code scanning alerts pours every field of every alert into the context; with gh-proxy and cli-proxy the agent works in bash, discovers each CLI through --help, writes the full response to a file and pipes out only the answer with jq, sort and head, so data grows on disk instead of in context. |
| inlined-skills-and-agents | Inlined Skills & Agents | illustrative | Defer detailed instructions into inline skills and delegate focused work to smaller-model agents, with real workflow examples showing both patterns in use. |
| audit-and-optimize | Audit & Optimize | illustrative | A health agent spots a failing or costly workflow, audits its unified session through the agentic-workflows skill, and tunes it so the next run is cheaper. |
| agentic-engineering | Agentic Engineering |  | Band header (Agentic Engineering): skip needless runs and give agents memory, hand-offs, expiry, search and measurement. |
| agents-that-debug-agents | Agents that debug agents | illustrative | The agentic-workflows MCP server exposes logs, audit and audit-diff so any agent can debug, audit and optimize other workflows from unified sessions. |

| fuzzy-schedules | Fuzzy schedules | illustrative | Fuzzy schedules such as daily hash each workflow to its own stable, off-peak time so runs never spike together; hourly, every N hours or minutes and weekly forms scatter too, while every N days and raw cron stay fixed; and the All You Can Eat pattern wakes often but skips while its last output is open, serving one item at a time as people consume them. |
| week-of-daily-runs | Week of daily runs |  | A measured week of gh-aw's daily workflows by weekday and UTC hour shows the fuzzy scatter at fleet scale: nothing runs at 00 or 01 UTC, the quiet 02 to 05 UTC hours carry the most, weekends lighten as weekday-only reports drop out, and no hour holds more than a small share of the fleet. |
